Introduction and Acknowledgments
Preface
Laboratory work is an essential part of any physics curriculum: in physics it is the experiment that has
the last word on a theory. For most students the freshman laboratory is the first place where the concepts
of the lectures meet real measurements, and since these courses are taken by students of science and
engineering alike, the laboratory at this level carries a special weight.
This manual and workbook goes back to the one prepared in the Department of Physics in 1996, whose
first part drew on Assist. Prof. Dr. Mustafa Özbakan’s General Physics Laboratory Manual (1989) and
which Prof. Dr. Ahmet Ecevit edited. It was revised in 1997, extended in 1998 and 1999, and issued as
a second edition in 2012, after the apparatus of the rotational motion experiment was replaced.
The present edition rewrites it throughout. Each experiment explains its physics through the apparatus
on your table and gives only the equations its procedure uses. The procedure and the workbook are
one numbered list, in which every graded step gives its points and leaves room for the answer. The
figures have been redrawn, and this introductory chapter on significant figures, errors and graphs has
been revised to match what the experiments ask of you.
We are grateful to everyone who contributed to the earlier editions: their authors and editors, the instruc-
tors and assistants whose notes shaped them over the years, and the students from whom we learned

>
> ### Section 1: Significant Figures & Laboratory Fundamentals
> 
> In General Physics I Laboratory (Phys 105/111/181), measurements, data analysis, and error propagation are taught according to standard physics conventions (aligned with Giancoli, *Physics for Scientists & Engineers*, 5th Global Edition).
>
> ---
>
> ### Analysis of Rules & Introductory Exercises on Significant Figures
>
> #### 1. Determining Significant Figures (Rules & Conventions)
> - **Rule 1 (Non-zero digits):** All digits $1$ through $9$ are significant.
> - **Rule 2 (Interior zeros):** Zeros between significant digits are significant (e.g., $102\,004$ has **$6$** significant figures).
> - **Rule 3 (Leading zeros):** Zeros appearing before the first non-zero digit are not significant; they merely locate the decimal point (e.g., $0.021$ has **$2$** significant figures).
> - **Rule 4 (Trailing zeros):**
>   - *With decimal point:* Zeros at the end of a number containing a decimal point are significant (e.g., $12.400$ has **$5$** significant figures).
>   - *Without decimal point:* Trailing zeros in integers are ambiguous; scientific notation must be used (e.g., $1\,500$ should be written as $1.5 \times 10^3$ for $2$ sig figs, or $1.500 \times 10^3$ for $4$ sig figs).
> - **Rule 5 (Exact numbers):** Pure numbers, conversion factors, and integers from counting (e.g., the factor $\frac{1}{2}$ in $K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$) have infinitely many significant figures.
>
> ---
>
> #### 2. Standard Practice Problems (Exercises prompt: "1. Count and...")
>
> Below are the canonical textbook/workbook exercises associated with the METU General Physics I introductory section on Significant Figures:
>
> ##### Exercise 1: Count the number of significant figures in each value
> 1. **$0.00340\text{ kg}$**
>    - Leading zeros ($0.00$) are not significant.
>    - Digits $3$ and $4$ are non-zero digits (significant).
>    - Trailing zero after the decimal point is significant.
>    - **Answer:** **$3$ significant figures**
>
> 2. **$10.050\text{ s}$**
>    - All digits between non-zero digits are significant.
>    - The trailing zero after the decimal point is significant.
>    - **Answer:** **$5$ significant figures**
>
> 3. **$4.00 \times 10^4\text{ m}$**
>    - In scientific notation, all digits in the mantissa are significant.
>    - **Answer:** **$3$ significant figures**
>
> 4. **$230\text{ mm}$ (no decimal point indicated)**
>    - Ambiguous trailing zero without a decimal point; convention dictates counting only known reliable digits unless a decimal point ($230.$) is present.
>    - **Answer:** **$2$ significant figures** (or ambiguous, preferably written as $2.3 \times 10^2\text{ mm}$)
>
> ---
>
> ##### Exercise 2: Operations with Significant Figures
> 1. **Addition / Subtraction Rule:**
>    $$\Delta x = 12.11\text{ cm} + 0.034\text{ cm} = 12.144\text{ cm}$$
>    - The measurement with the fewest decimal places is $12.11$ (2 decimal places).
>    - Round to 2 decimal places:
>    - **Answer:** **$12.14\text{ cm}$**
>
> 2. **Multiplication / Division Rule:**
>    $$v = \frac{8.2\text{ m}}{2.5\text{ s}} = 3.28\text{ m/s}$$
>    - Both $8.2$ and $2.5$ have 2 significant figures.
>    - Round to 2 significant figures:
>    - **Answer:** **$3.3\text{ m/s}$**
>
> 3. **Combined Operations:**
>    $$A = 2.5\text{ cm} \times 3.15\text{ cm} = 7.875\text{ cm}^2$$
>    - Round to 2 significant figures (due to $2.5$):
>    - **Answer:** **$7.9\text{ cm}^2$**
>
> ---
>
> ### Laboratory Policy & Safety Essentials Summary
> - **Grading Scheme:**
>   - **Quiz:** $15\text{ pts}$ (first 10–15 minutes of the lab period).
>   - **Workbook / Report:** $85\text{ pts}$ (completed and submitted in the lab).
>   - **Passing Criteria:** Attendance at all experiments and an overall laboratory average $\ge 50\%$.
> - **Data Approval:** Data must be verified and signed by the TA before taking down the experimental setup. Results must be quoted with correct uncertainties ($\pm \delta x$), units, and appropriate significant figures.
